notes: The US Food and Drug Administration regulates medical devices, including their cybersecurity. Its guidance documents are non-binding recommendations that describe FDA's current thinking, but in practice they set the expectations a premarket submission is reviewed against. Section 524B of the FD&C Act (added by the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023) made cybersecurity information a statutory submission requirement for 'cyber devices' — the binding obligation is the statute; these documents are how FDA says it will be met. All FDA guidance is US Government work and in the public domain.

match_nodes.description: Cybersecurity in Medical Devices: Quality System Considerations and Content of Premarket Submissions

data.official_name: Cybersecurity in Medical Devices: Quality System Considerations and Content of Premarket Submissions (final guidance, September 2023)
data.notes: FDA's premarket cybersecurity expectations. Supersedes the 2014 and draft 2018 premarket guidance. Covers the Secure Product Development Framework, threat modeling, a software bill of materials, and the cybersecurity information a submission must contain under FD&C Act section 524B. Compensating controls are accepted but scrutinised — FDA expects the residual risk after controls to be justified, not merely asserted.

match_nodes.description: Postmarket Management of Cybersecurity in Medical Devices

data.official_name: Postmarket Management of Cybersecurity in Medical Devices (final guidance, December 2016)
data.notes: FDA's expectations for devices already on the market: monitoring, vulnerability intake, and remediation. Turns on the distinction between **controlled** and **uncontrolled risk** — a compensating control can move a device to controlled risk and thereby avoid the reporting and recall obligations that uncontrolled risk triggers. That determination is the practical decision point for medical device vulnerability response, and it is reached through the ISO 14971 risk process (secid:control/iso.org/14971).
